ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection of Oklahoma City, OK piping, vessels, tanks and power plant steel, done on your site. Request a UT quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing and UT Inspection in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT provides ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld examination for industrial owners in Oklahoma City and the surrounding metro: gathering and processing piping, vessels and tanks, power plant systems, plant utilities and fabricated steel. Technicians are mobilized to the site with flaw detectors, thickness gauges, probes and calibration blocks, and they report against the code or specification you name. Send a request for an ultrasonic testing quote and a reply comes within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Oklahoma City

Oklahoma City's industrial base is broader than its reputation as an oil town suggests. Energy remains central: the metro is home to exploration and production companies and an electric utility, and production from the surrounding basins moves through gathering lines, compressor stations, separators, treaters and saltwater handling facilities. Aerospace is the other pillar, with a large Air Force depot maintenance complex at Tinker Air Force Base, the FAA's Mike Monroney Aeronautical Center, and commercial aerospace suppliers. Manufacturing and distribution add equipment makers, building products plants, HVAC and controls producers, and aggregate operations.

For ultrasonic work that translates into jobs such as:

  • Wall readings on production piping, free-water knockouts, heater treaters and scrubbers in central Oklahoma oil and gas service.
  • Thickness checks on compressor station piping and bottles, where pulsation and wet gas thin the wall at elbows and low points.
  • Boiler tube, steam piping and feedwater system readings in power generation and large facility heating plants.
  • Thickness grids on aboveground storage tanks, including water and chemical tanks in industrial parks.
  • Weld examination on fabricated pressure equipment and structural steel built in metro fabrication shops.
  • Base-plate, lug and thickness verification on ground support structures, hangar steel and fuel storage at aviation and military sites, where owners permit it.

What an ultrasonic examination can and cannot tell you

Ultrasonics sends sound into steel and listens for echoes. The delay of the back-wall echo converts to thickness, and an echo from somewhere inside the wall or weld flags a reflector. That is why it is the working tool for remaining wall: no other common method gives a number for how much metal is left from one side only.

Its weaknesses come from the physics. The sound has to enter the metal, so rough, scaled or coated surfaces degrade readings, and couplant must bridge the gap. Rapidly changing geometry, such as the inside of a small-radius elbow, bends the beam in ways that make thickness readings uncertain. Coarse-grained material, including some castings and weld metal, scatters the sound. A flaw whose face lies parallel to the beam reflects almost nothing back, so weld flaws are scanned from more than one angle and direction. Pits are the most frequent source of error: the probe face is larger than a pit, so a reading may land beside the deepest point. Technicians scan an area and report the minimum rather than relying on one spot.

Codes, state rules and acceptance criteria

The technique requirements come from ASME Section V: Article 5 for materials, Article 4 for welds, and Article 23, where SE-797 covers contact pulse-echo thickness measurement. ASTM E797 is the practice for general use, and ASTM E164 covers contact examination of weldments. Weld acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for vessels, ASME B31.3 and its Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, and API 1104 for pipeline welding. Bridge steel in Oklahoma follows AWS D1.5.

The Oklahoma Department of Labor's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Service oversees boilers, other pressure vessels and the firms that install and repair them. Its inspections are performed by the state or by authorized insurance companies, and inspectors must hold a National Board commission, so thickness data on jurisdictional equipment is often read by those inspectors. For in-service equipment under API 510, 570 or 653 the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record. Atlantis delivers the readings and the report, not the fitness-for-service decision. Pipeline operators work under PHMSA's 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, and plants with large inventories of hazardous chemicals follow OSHA's 29 CFR 1910.119 mechanical integrity requirements.

Technique in the field

A thickness survey begins with calibration. The technician sets the instrument on a step block made of the same alloy as the part, brackets the expected wall range, and confirms the reading at both ends of the survey. A dual-element probe is the default on corroded steel because it handles pitted surfaces better, and the A-scan is displayed on pitted or thin wall so that a premature echo or a doubled signal is recognized and not blindly recorded. For warm surfaces, such as steam or process lines, a high-temperature probe and couplant are used and the reading is corrected for temperature.

Weld examination uses angle-beam shear wave probes, typically at forty-five, sixty or seventy degrees, selected for wall thickness and joint design. A distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes, and the weld is scanned from both sides where geometry allows. Indications above the recording level are evaluated for length, position and amplitude, then compared with the code. Details of probe choice and calibration are in our ultrasonic testing guide, and the Article 5 thickness requirements explainer covers the thickness side.

Reading corrosion rate from two surveys

A single thickness reading tells you the wall today; two readings at the same place tell you how fast it is going. Owners in Oklahoma City who run gathering and treating equipment tend to care about the rate more than the number, because produced water, carbon dioxide and sulfur compounds change from well to well and season to season. We lay out survey points so they can be found again, mark them on a sketch, and where earlier data exists we compare like with like. A short-term rate uses the last interval, a long-term rate uses the original or baseline wall, and the report shows both so the authorized inspector can decide which governs.

Calculated remaining life is the owner's decision, not ours, since it depends on corrosion allowance, operating conditions and the applicable inspection code. What we owe is data that is trustworthy: calibrated, repeatable and clearly tied to its location.

Examining fabricated welds before they leave the shop

Oklahoma City has a steady base of fabrication shops building skids, tanks, pressure vessels and structural packages for energy, utility and building-products customers. Ultrasonic weld examination at the shop catches lack of fusion and cracking while repair is still cheap, long before the equipment is loaded on a truck. We scan to the construction code, often alongside the shop's own quality staff, and the report states the acceptance criteria applied. Shops that need independent verification of a customer-specified examination can request it ahead of delivery.

Who carries out the work

Atlantis technicians work through a written practice modeled on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician calibrates, performs and interprets; an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Because SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based practice, the employer certifies its personnel, and Atlantis will share the written practice for customer review. Atlantis has no office in Oklahoma City. Technicians travel to your site, and safety orientation, gate access and permit steps are arranged with you before they mobilize. If you have a company UT procedure, we review it and work to it. Our Level III consulting and written practice development pages describe the oversight side.

What the ultrasonic report contains

Every report states what was examined and how. Equipment is identified by tag, line or drawing number, the procedure and revision are named, and the governing code and acceptance criteria are stated. The instrument, probe, couplant and calibration block are listed with calibration checks, and the technician name and level appear alongside surface condition and temperature.

Thickness surveys include a grid or sketch with each reading, nominal and minimum wall where provided, and highlighted points below the threshold. Weld reports list each recordable indication with location, length, depth and amplitude and give an accept or reject finding. The file is organized so an authorized inspector, insurer or auditor can follow it without a phone call.

Planning ultrasonic work in Oklahoma City

Oklahoma weather swings widely. Summer afternoons are hot and windy, which dries couplant fast and heats steel until probe wear and temperature corrections matter. Winter brings freezing mornings and the occasional ice storm that can close roads and delay outdoor work. Spring severe weather, including thunderstorms and tornado warnings, can halt work at short notice, so outdoor jobs benefit from schedule flexibility and a shelter plan at the site.

Most of the preparation is logistical. Insulation removal, scaffolding and cleaning drive the schedule on thickness surveys, so say who provides them. Federal and military sites impose access and escort rules that add lead time, and gas plants and power stations have their own orientation. Send us the equipment list, drawings, nominal wall, the governing code and earlier readings; we then propose the scope, the number of readings and the report format. Plan around known outages, as turnaround seasons draw heavily on the same pool of technicians.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT in Oklahoma City

Use ultrasonics when the question is remaining wall, corrosion rate or the soundness of a weld through its thickness. If the question is whether a carbon steel weld toe has a surface crack, magnetic particle inspection in Oklahoma City is the quicker and more sensitive choice. If the metal is stainless, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy, liquid penetrant testing in Oklahoma City does that job. Repairs often use two methods: ultrasonics for remaining wall and weld volume, and a surface method for the final weld. For the broader picture see inspection services across Oklahoma and the national UT page.

Building your own UT capability

Owners who want in-house skills can use UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator for scanning practice. The employer then certifies its own people. For local options, see NDT training for Oklahoma City.

faq.q: What equipment in Oklahoma City is typically measured with ultrasonic thickness testing?
faq.a: Production and gathering piping, separators, compressor station piping, boiler tubes and steam lines, storage tanks and fabricated vessels are common. Anything where internal corrosion or erosion thins the wall is a candidate for a repeatable thickness survey.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing evaluate a weld without cutting it open?
faq.a: Yes. Angle-beam shear wave probes send sound through the weld at a set angle, and echoes from lack of fusion, cracks or slag show on the display. Indications are located, sized and compared with the acceptance criteria of the construction code.

faq.q: Why does pitting make ultrasonic readings harder?
faq.a: A probe face is wider than most pits, so the reading can land on sound metal beside a deep pit and overstate the wall. Technicians scan across the area and record the lowest value, and they watch the A-scan for unstable or premature echoes.

faq.q: Is it possible to test hot piping with ultrasonics?
faq.a: Often yes. High-temperature probes and couplant allow readings on warm lines, and the instrument is corrected for the temperature effect. Very hot surfaces are limited by contact time, and we agree the limits with you before starting.

faq.q: How do Oklahoma Department of Labor rules affect my thickness data?
faq.a: State inspectors, who hold National Board commissions, oversee boilers and many pressure vessels, so thickness records on jurisdictional equipment may be reviewed by them or an authorized insurer. We write the report so the data and calibration are traceable.

faq.q: Does Atlantis serve as the authorized inspector under API 510, 570 or 653?
faq.a: No. The owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection program and fitness-for-service decisions. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and supplies the data and report that inspector uses.

faq.q: What information do I send to get an ultrasonic quote?
faq.a: Send the equipment or line list, drawings, nominal and minimum wall values, the governing code, access limits, and any previous thickness records. Use the quote link on this page and a reply arrives within one business day.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Oklahoma City?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad. Technicians are mobilized to your Oklahoma City site for the agreed scope, with gate access, orientation and permits arranged beforehand.

faq.q: Can my team learn UT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training and a Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A your own company certifies your technicians against its written practice after the training and experience hours are met.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Oklahoma City, OK
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing of Oklahoma City, OK welds, skids, rigging and fabricated steel, done at your site. Request an MT quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma
mt.html:
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI, or mag particle testing) locates surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to industrial sites across Oklahoma City to examine welds, lugs, rigging, structural connections and repair excavations. We bring yokes, particles, a light meter and field indicators, work to a written procedure, and report indications against your code. Request a magnetic particle inspection quote through the link and expect a reply within one business day.

Why steel in the Oklahoma City area needs surface crack checks

Central Oklahoma runs on welded carbon steel. Oil and gas production in the nearby basins relies on skids, separators, flowlines and compressors that are welded in shops across the metro and repaired in the field. Rail and truck distribution centers, building products and equipment makers fabricate and weld steel assemblies. The aerospace and defense sector, centered on Tinker Air Force Base, runs ground equipment, hangar structures, jigs and handling fixtures, much of it carbon steel that is lifted, loaded and cycled.

Mag particle inspection comes up in places like these:

  • Weld toes and attachment welds on production separators, treaters and pressure vessel supports.
  • Skid frames and compressor package structures after modification or cracking from vibration.
  • Crane hooks, shackles, slings hardware, spreader beams and lifting fixtures used in yards and plants.
  • Trailer frames, truck-mounted equipment and heavy hauling components where fatigue cracks begin at welds.
  • Structural connections on pipe racks, platforms and equipment towers.
  • Ground-out repair areas, examined to prove the crack is removed before rewelding.

What mag particle testing reveals, and the gaps in what it reveals

When a magnetic field passes through steel, a crack across the field forces some flux out of the surface. Fine iron particles applied over the area collect at that leakage and draw a visible line along the flaw. The method is quick, works through thin coatings in some cases, and is very sensitive to tight cracks that other surface methods can miss.

There are firm boundaries. Austenitic stainless, aluminum, copper alloys and other non-magnetic materials cannot be examined this way, however good the surface. Sensitivity falls steeply with depth, so only surface and shallowly subsurface flaws appear, and nothing about wall thickness or deep flaws. A flaw is detectable only when it lies across the field, and a crack running along the field lines produces almost no leakage, which is why two field directions are used. Coatings thicker than the procedure allows reduce leakage and can mask indications. Non-relevant indications from changes in section or magnetic writing may appear and must be sorted from real flaws.

Codes that govern magnetic particle work

ASME Section V Article 7 sets the method requirements, supported by ASTM E709 and the practice ASTM E1444. For acceptance, the construction code controls. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 applies to vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 to process piping, ASME B31.1 to power piping, and AWS D1.1 to structural welds. State bridge steel falls under AWS D1.5.

In Oklahoma the Department of Labor's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Service regulates boilers and many pressure vessels, requires permits for new installations, and relies on inspectors with National Board commissions. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code. Under API 510, 570 and 653, the owner's authorized inspector accepts or rejects findings and sets repair requirements; Atlantis reports the indications. Process plants under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 keep these records as mechanical integrity evidence. See the Article 7 explainer for what the standard asks of the technician.

Technique: field direction, particles and light

Most field work uses an electromagnetic yoke that is checked for lifting power before use: Article 7 asks for at least ten pounds for an AC yoke and forty pounds for DC or permanent magnet yokes at the spacing used. Dry powder suits rough or warm weld surfaces, and wet particles in a visible or fluorescent suspension reveal finer cracks on smoother steel. Fluorescent work is viewed under UV-A light in a dark area and the light intensity and ambient light are measured. White contrast paint helps visible particles show against dark steel.

Direction is verified with a pie gauge or shim indicator. The technician applies particles while the field is active, examines the weld, then repeats with the yoke rotated to roughly ninety degrees. Where the geometry or thickness calls for it the procedure may specify prods, a coil or a central conductor. Afterward the part is demagnetized if the residual field would affect welding, machining, instrument accuracy or service. The complete magnetic particle guide and the national MT service page add detail.

Preparing the surface for mag particle work

Particles need to move freely and the yoke needs a good contact patch. Loose scale, spatter, heavy rust and thick paint are removed where the procedure requires, and oil and grease are cleaned off equipment that has been in service. For wet fluorescent work, cleanliness matters even more because residue glows under UV light and hides small indications. Surface condition is noted in the report, so a clean result is read with the context that produced it.

Examples of how mag particle findings drive decisions

A magnetic particle result is rarely the end of the story. On a lifting fixture, a linear indication at a weld toe means the fixture is removed from service until repaired and re-examined, since fatigue cracks grow under load. On a skid frame, a crack at a gusset might lead the owner to add reinforcement as well as repair the weld, because the same stress that started the crack will start another. On a pressure vessel support, the finding goes to the authorized inspector, who decides whether the crack is repaired under the National Board Inspection Code or whether the item is replaced.

Because the technician sees the part in the condition it will be released in, the report also records negatives. A clean weld toe on a rigging lug, documented with the procedure, field direction and date, is evidence that the part was checked before it went back to work, and that is valuable when a load test or an audit asks later.

Rope, rigging and heavy-lift considerations

Heavy hauling and lifting are part of daily life at yards, distribution centers and fabrication shops around Oklahoma City, and hardware that is stressed daily is the first place fatigue appears. Examination of hooks, shackles, eyebolts and spreader bars is usually done with a yoke and either wet or dry particles after the surface has been cleaned of grease. We also examine around welded attachments on crane runways and trailers. If a part is cracked, we mark it and report immediately so it is tagged out, and the written record names the item so no one reuses it by mistake.

Who does the examination

Technicians are qualified through an Atlantis written practice founded on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians set up the equipment, perform the examination and interpret indications, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. As SNT-TC-1A is employer-based, the employer certifies its own people, and the written practice is available for customer review. Atlantis has no office in Oklahoma City, so technicians travel to your site, and we line up orientation, gate access and permits before the job. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, oversees the Level III function. If you want your own procedure reviewed, see Level III consulting.

What the magnetic particle report records

The report names the component and location, the procedure and its revision, the code and acceptance criteria, and the technique: yoke type, wet or dry particles, visible or fluorescent, and the field directions used. It lists the lifting-power check, the light measurements for fluorescent work, surface condition, temperature, date and the technician and level.

Each recordable indication is entered with position, orientation and length, with a sketch or photograph where needed, and an accept or reject finding against the named criteria. Where a flaw is removed by grinding, the follow-up examination of the excavation is recorded too. Such a file answers the questions an authorized inspector or insurer will ask later about how a repair was verified.

Practical planning for Oklahoma City sites

Oklahoma conditions affect the job. Hot, windy summer afternoons dry wet suspensions quickly and make surfaces too warm for some particle carriers. Winter ice and cold slow cleaning and drying, and spring storms can interrupt outdoor work with little notice. Fluorescent examination needs a darkened area, which means a tent or a shaded bay when working in daylight.

Give us the base metal, coating, weld type, extent of examination and governing code, and tell us whether hot work or confined space permits apply. Tinker and other federal sites require access screening that can add lead time, and plants impose their own orientation. Early notice helps us match equipment and personnel to your outage window.

Choosing between MT, PT and UT in Oklahoma City

Pick magnetic particle inspection for surface cracks in ferromagnetic welds. For stainless steel or aluminum, liquid penetrant testing in Oklahoma City is the surface method. When the question is wall thickness or the interior of a weld, ultrasonic testing in Oklahoma City is the one that answers it. The MT versus PT comparison is a quick guide, and the Oklahoma inspection services hub collects the state's pages.

Developing your own MT staff

If you want in-house skills, Atlantis teaches MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and your company certifies its technicians under its written practice. See NDT training for Oklahoma City and check SNT-TC-1A eligibility for experience requirements.

faq.q: Which Oklahoma City materials can be examined by magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Carbon steel and most low-alloy steels, because they are ferromagnetic. Stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys are not, so surface cracks in those need liquid penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: How deep can magnetic particle inspection see?
faq.a: Only at and just under the surface. Sensitivity drops quickly with depth, so deep internal flaws are missed. For internal weld flaws or remaining wall, ultrasonic testing is the appropriate method.

faq.q: Why is the part examined twice at right angles?
faq.a: A crack shows only when it crosses the magnetic field. If the first direction runs along a flaw it may not appear, so the code requires a second examination with the field rotated by roughly ninety degrees.

faq.q: Is fluorescent magnetic particle testing done outdoors?
faq.a: It can be, but only with a darkened work area such as a tent or shaded bay, because the UV-A light must dominate over ambient white light. Visible particles are usually chosen when darkness is hard to provide.

faq.q: Do I have to strip paint from the weld before examination?
faq.a: Thin, tight coatings may remain if the procedure shows that indications are still reliably produced. Thick or flaking coatings are removed. We test sensitivity on a representative sample before accepting the coating.

faq.q: When is demagnetization required?
faq.a: When leftover magnetism could disturb arc welding, machining, instruments or moving parts. The technician measures the residual field after inspection and demagnetizes if it exceeds the limit in the procedure.

faq.q: Can you inspect crane and rigging hardware?
faq.a: Yes. Hooks, shackles, lugs and lifting beams are common mag particle jobs, since fatigue cracks start at welds and stress points. The report records the part identity and the accept or reject outcome against your specification.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Oklahoma City?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad, and none in Oklahoma City. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, with access screening, orientation and permits arranged beforehand.

faq.q: Who is responsible for certifying the technicians?
faq.a: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies personnel. Atlantis qualifies its technicians through its written practice, with Level II performing and interpreting and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Oklahoma City, OK
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection of stainless, aluminum and alloy welds in Oklahoma City, OK, done at your site. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma
pt.html:
Liquid penetrant testing, known on the shop floor as dye penetrant inspection or PT, shows cracks and porosity that break the surface of a part, in magnetic and non-magnetic metals alike. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to facilities across Oklahoma City to examine stainless piping, aluminum structures, alloy welds, castings and repair areas. Request a dye penetrant inspection quote and a reply comes within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in the Oklahoma City metro

Oklahoma City's mix of aerospace, energy and manufacturing produces plenty of metal that magnets cannot test. Aerospace support work around Tinker Air Force Base and the FAA's Aeronautical Center involves aluminum structures, stainless fittings and alloy hardware. Energy sector equipment includes stainless and duplex piping in treating and chemical injection systems, plus aluminum cooler fins and fabricated parts. Heating, cooling and controls manufacturers weld copper, aluminum and stainless assemblies, and distribution and equipment makers join a wide range of alloys.

Examples include:

  • Weld root and cap examination on stainless steel and alloy piping used in chemical injection and treating.
  • Aluminum welds on trailers, tank bodies, platforms and handling equipment.
  • Machined and cast parts, such as valve bodies, pump housings and fittings, checked for surface porosity or cracks.
  • Heat exchanger nozzle and shell welds in stainless or alloy steel.
  • Carbon steel welds with awkward geometry where a magnetic yoke cannot seat.
  • Reexamination of ground-out areas to confirm a defect has been removed.

What penetrant testing can find, and what it cannot

The process is simple in principle. A liquid with high capillary action is placed on a clean surface, enters any opening, and is then removed from the surface. A developer pulls the trapped liquid back out, so the flaw appears as a bright or colored line that is much wider than the crack itself. Because it relies on capillary action and not magnetism, the method is available on practically every non-porous material.

But the discontinuity must reach the surface. A crack sealed by smeared metal from grinding, shot blasting or machining never takes up penetrant, and contamination such as oil, paint or scale hides it as effectively. Rough, porous or rusty surfaces hold penetrant and give a broad background that masks real indications. Penetrant says nothing about flaws below the surface or the thickness of the wall. For those questions another method is needed, and for surface cracks in carbon steel welds a magnetic method is often more productive.

Codes and acceptance for penetrant examination

ASME Section V Article 6 sets the technique requirements and ASTM E165 is the general practice. Acceptance is defined by the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, and AWS D1.1 or D1.6 for structural carbon and stainless steel welding. Owners may add stricter criteria.

The Oklahoma Department of Labor's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Service regulates boilers and pressure vessels, with inspections by the state or an authorized insurer and National Board commissioned inspectors; repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code. For in-service API 510, 570 and 653 equipment, the owner's authorized inspector accepts the findings, and Atlantis provides the examination data. OSHA's 29 CFR 1910.119 expects mechanical integrity records at covered plants. The Article 6 explainer covers the requirements in more detail.

Technique, step by step

The procedure controls every step. The technician cleans the area to remove oil, scale, paint and spatter, then dries it fully. Penetrant is applied by spray, brush or dip and left to dwell for the time stated in the procedure, which depends on the material, the flaw sought and the temperature. Excess is removed by the method named, whether water washable, solvent removable or post-emulsifiable, then a thin, even coat of developer is applied and given time to draw out indications.

Visible dye, usually red, is read under white light and is the field standard. Fluorescent penetrant is read under UV-A light in a dark area and offers more sensitivity for critical work. The technician interprets within the time window set by the procedure and distinguishes relevant indications from non-relevant ones such as bleed-out from a scratch or weld ripple. On the matter of temperature, the code's standard range applies to ordinary shop-type conditions and the procedure must be qualified for anything outside it. See MT versus PT for help choosing, and the national penetrant testing page for the method overview.

Selecting and controlling the penetrant materials

A penetrant job begins with the right family of materials. Type I fluorescent and Type II visible systems differ in sensitivity, and methods A, B, C and D differ in how excess penetrant is removed. Field work on welds commonly uses solvent-removable visible materials because they are portable and controllable, while shop work on castings may use washable fluorescent systems. Owners who work with stainless steel and nickel alloys often limit the chlorine, fluorine and sulfur in the materials so that residues cannot attack the metal; we check batch certificates against those limits, and we confirm the materials are not mixed between families.

Reference panels or comparators show whether the system is producing fine indications on the day, and the developer is inspected for contamination. If the check shows poor response, the materials or the process are corrected before production parts are examined.

Cleaning and surface preparation for PT

Most penetrant failures start before any liquid is applied. Surfaces are usually examined as welded or after light dressing, but slag, spatter and oxide must be removed so they cannot bridge a flaw. Where machining, grinding or blasting has smeared metal across the opening, the procedure may require an etch or other step to reopen it. After cleaning, the part must be completely dry, because trapped solvent or water blocks a crack just as dirt does. We record how the surface was prepared, since that affects how much confidence a clean result deserves.

Reading indications correctly

Not every bleed-out is a flaw. Tool marks, scratches, weld ripple and sharp transitions can trap penetrant and mimic cracks. The technician judges shape, location and the way the bleed-out grows as the developer dries, then wipes the spot, reapplies developer and looks again. Linear indications at a weld toe or crater are treated as possible cracks, while rounded ones are sized against the criteria. If an indication is borderline, the report says so and the owner or a Level III decides whether a light dressing and retest, or a different method, is the right next step.

PT on aluminum and stainless in aerospace-related work

Facilities connected to aviation and defense often work in aluminum and stainless, where cracks begin at fasteners, welds and sharp corners. For ground equipment, tooling, fixtures and structural hardware on the owner's site, penetrant testing provides a surface check that does not depend on magnetism. Atlantis offers it as an industrial inspection service for that hardware, under the owner's procedure or one we write for the job, and does not perform aircraft airworthiness examinations.

Who performs the work

Penetrant technicians work through Atlantis's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform the examination and interpret indications; an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. As the employer certifies its own people under that recommended practice, the written practice is open to customer review. Atlantis has no office in Oklahoma City, and technicians travel to your site once access, orientation and chemical approvals are arranged. Where you have a site procedure we review it and work to it. For related services see written practice development.

What the penetrant report includes

The report names the component, material and area examined, the procedure and revision, and the acceptance criteria. It records the penetrant system by type and method, with cleaner and developer, the dwell and development times, and the surface and ambient temperatures. The technician and level, date and extent of examination are included.

Each indication is entered with its location, shape and size, labelled relevant or non-relevant, and photographed or sketched if helpful. Findings are marked accept or reject against the named criteria, and follow-up examinations after grinding or repair are reported in the same way. The record is ready to join a repair package or quality file.

Planning a penetrant job in Oklahoma City

The weather is a practical constraint. Direct sun on a steel surface during an Oklahoma summer can push it above the standard temperature range, which flashes off cleaner and penetrant before it has time to work. Cold winter mornings slow the dwell and make developer behave unpredictably, and wind carries dust that contaminates prepared surfaces. When the surface is outside the range we shade, warm or cool the part, or use a procedure qualified for the actual temperature. Storms and severe weather can end an outdoor day with little warning.

Cleaning often takes longer than the examination, and cleaners need site approval and ventilation. Tell us the material, any coating, the weld type, the code, and whether chloride or sulfur limits apply. Federal and military sites require access screening that adds lead time, and plants add their own orientation. Early notice lets us fit your outage window.

Choosing between PT, MT and UT in Oklahoma City

Use penetrant testing for surface-breaking flaws in non-magnetic materials and on parts where a yoke will not seat. For carbon steel welds, magnetic particle inspection in Oklahoma City is often faster. When remaining wall or the inside of a weld is the question, ultrasonic testing in Oklahoma City is the method to use. Combined packages are common. Read the Oklahoma inspection services hub for more.

faq.q: What does dye penetrant inspection detect in Oklahoma City equipment?
faq.a: It detects cracks, laps, seams and porosity that open to the surface of a part. It works on stainless steel, aluminum and many other non-magnetic metals, as well as carbon steel, but it cannot see flaws below the surface.

faq.q: Why is penetrant testing used on aluminum and stainless steel?
faq.a: Because it depends on capillary action and not magnetism, so it works on any non-porous material. Magnetic particle inspection cannot examine those metals, which makes penetrant the standard surface method for them.

faq.q: What can stop penetrant from finding a crack?
faq.a: Anything that blocks the opening: oil, paint, scale, spatter, or metal smeared closed by grinding or blasting. That is why cleaning is part of the examination and why some procedures restrict mechanical cleaning before testing.

faq.q: How do temperature and weather affect penetrant testing?
faq.a: Surfaces that are too hot flash off the liquids before they work, and cold slows the dwell and development. The code's standard range is moderate, so we check surface temperature and shade, warm or use a qualified procedure when it falls outside.

faq.q: Which is better, visible or fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Neither is universally better. Visible red dye is practical in the field under normal light, while fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive but needs UV-A light in a dark area. The procedure or the owner's specification decides.

faq.q: Do you control chlorine and sulfur on stainless steel?
faq.a: We check batch certificates against any limits the owner specifies for halogens and sulfur on stainless and nickel alloys, and we record the materials used so the file shows the limits were met.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects the findings on in-service equipment?
faq.a: For API 510, 570 and 653 equipment, the owner's authorized inspector decides. Atlantis performs the penetrant examination, records each indication and reports the technique so that inspector can rule on the results.
